“You can be sure they were all perfectly comfortable.”

“Perhaps that wouldn’t make me like them any better. So many women and children have no right to be comfortable aboard a ship.”

“My dear Frederick, you’re talking nonsense. What would happen to us poor sailors’ wives, who often need to travel from port to port to join our husbands, if everyone felt as you do?”

“As you see, my feelings didn’t stop me taking Mrs. Harville and her whole family to Plymouth.”

“But I hate hearing you talk like some grand gentleman, as though all women were delicate ladies instead of sensible human beings. None of us expects smooth sailing all our lives.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “he’ll change his tune when he has a wife. Once he’s married, if we’re lucky enough to live to see another war, he’ll do what you and I and plenty of others have done. We’ll find him very grateful to anyone who brings his wife to him.”

“Yes, we certainly will.”

“Now I give up,” Captain Wentworth exclaimed. “Once married people start attacking me with ‘Oh, you’ll think very differently when you’re married,’ all I can say is ‘No, I won’t.’ Then they say ‘Yes, you will,’ and that ends the discussion.”

He stood up and moved away.

“You must have traveled a great deal, ma’am!” Mrs. Musgrove said to Mrs. Croft.

“A fair amount, ma’am, in my fifteen years of marriage, although many women have traveled more. I’ve crossed the Atlantic four times and been to the East Indies and back once—only once. Then there are places nearer home: Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I’ve never gone beyond the straits, and I’ve never been to the West Indies. We don’t count Bermuda or the Bahamas as the West Indies, you know.”

Mrs. Musgrove had nothing to say against this. She could not accuse herself of ever having called them anything at all in her entire life.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” Mrs. Croft continued, “nothing could be more comfortable than the accommodation on a warship. I mean the larger classes, of course. On a frigate, naturally, you have less room, although any sensible woman can be perfectly happy on one. I can safely say that the happiest part of my life has been spent aboard a ship. As long as we were together, you know, there was nothing to fear.

People thought him a marvelous reader. At the church’s social gatherings he was invariably invited to recite poetry; and afterward the ladies would raise their hands, drop them limply into their laps, roll their eyes, and shake their heads, as though saying, “No words can describe it; it is too lovely, TOO lovely for this earthly world.”

Once the hymn was finished, the Reverend Mr. Sprague made himself into a notice-board, announcing meetings and societies and other matters until the catalogue seemed likely to continue to Judgment Day—a curious practice still maintained in America, even in cities, in this present age when newspapers abound. Often the fewer reasons there are for preserving an inherited custom, the more difficult it proves to abolish.

Then the minister began to pray. It was a fine, lavish prayer, with no lack of particulars. He pleaded for his church and its small children; for the village’s other churches; for the village; for the county; for the State and its officers; for the United States; for all the nation’s churches; for Congress; for the President; for the Government’s officers; for unfortunate sailors battered by tempestuous seas; for the millions groaning beneath the oppression of Europe’s monarchies and the despotisms of the East; for those who possessed the light and the glad tidings but lacked eyes to see or ears to hear; for the heathens on distant islands in the ocean. He concluded by asking that his forthcoming words might be received with grace and favor and resemble seed planted in rich soil, bringing forth, in due season, a welcome harvest of goodness. Amen.

Dresses rustled as the congregation, which had been standing, resumed its seats. The boy whose adventures are told in this book took no pleasure in the prayer; he merely suffered through it—if he managed even that. He fidgeted from beginning to end, keeping unconscious count of its particulars. He was not listening, but he knew the territory well and the minister’s customary path across it. Whenever a scrap of unfamiliar material was slipped in, however, his ear caught it and his whole being rebelled. He thought additions dishonest and downright villainous. Halfway through the prayer, a fly settled on the back of the pew ahead of him and tormented his soul by rubbing its hands together with perfect composure. It clasped its head between its arms and polished so energetically that the head seemed nearly to detach from its body, revealing the threadlike neck. With its hind legs it scraped its wings, then smoothed them against its body like the tails of a coat. It completed its entire toilette as peacefully as though it knew itself to be beyond danger.

It was early February. Anne had spent a month in Bath and was becoming very anxious for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted to know much more than Mary had told her, and three weeks had passed without any news at all. She knew only that Henrietta had returned home and that Louisa, although said to be recovering quickly, was still at Lyme. One evening, while Anne was thinking intently about them all, a letter from Mary arrived, thicker than usual. Adding to her pleasure and surprise, it came with Admiral and Mrs. Croft’s compliments.

The Crofts must be in Bath! That was interesting news. They were people she naturally felt fond of.

“What’s this?” Sir Walter exclaimed. “The Crofts have come to Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they brought you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, sir.”

“Oh! Those letters are useful passports. They ensure an introduction. Still, I would have visited Admiral Croft in any case. I know what I owe my tenant.”

Anne stopped listening. She could not even have said whether the poor Admiral’s complexion escaped criticism, for the letter held all her attention. Mary had begun it several days earlier.

“February 1st.

“MY DEAR ANNE,

I won’t apologize for not writing, because I know how little people care about letters somewhere like Bath. You must be far too happy to bother about Uppercross, where, as you know perfectly well, there is very little to write about. Christmas has been terribly dull. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove haven’t held a single dinner party throughout the holidays. I don’t count the Hayters as anybody. At least the holidays are finally over. I don’t believe any children have ever had such long ones; I certainly never did. The house emptied yesterday, apart from the little Harvilles. You’ll be surprised to hear they still haven’t gone home. Mrs. Harville must be a strange sort of mother to let them stay away so long. I can’t understand it. I don’t think they’re nice children at all, but Mrs. Musgrove seems to like them quite as much as her own grandchildren, if not more. What dreadful weather we’ve had! Perhaps you don’t notice it in Bath, with your nice pavements, but it matters in the country. Nobody has visited me since the second week of January except Charles Hayter, who has been coming much more often than anyone wants. Between ourselves, I think it’s a great pity Henrietta didn’t stay in Lyme as long as Louisa. It would have kept her away from him a little.
